_comment: Catalogues a codebase's allocator surface organised BY DEALLOCATOR FAMILY: each
`families` entry is ONE free/deallocator plus the FLAT list of routines whose
output it releases. Every buffer-producer is one `allocators[]` entry - a plain
allocation, a resize (`realloc`, a `(ptr,size)` signature), or a duplicator
(`*strdup`/`*memdup`) alike - with the operation read from its `type` signature
and qualifier flags, NOT an explicit `op` tag. An allocator may appear under
MORE THAN ONE family when its output can be released by more than one
deallocator (e.g. a plain free and a clearing free - distinct families because
the wrapper's drop strategy is fixed by which C free it calls). Non-allocating
copies (`memcpy`) that write into a CALLER-owned dest are attached to each
family's `copies[]` (the families whose buffers they fill). Plus `refcounts`,
`locks`, `cleansers`. Macro variants are RESOLVED to the underlying symbols they
expand to (FFI never calls macros). Downstream: the buffer pass of
strings/arrays type-wrapper prompts, lifecycle classification. Values are
GENERIC (libc + a fictional `proj_*` layer) illustrating every archetype; a real
run substitutes the target's symbols, one family per deallocator.
_comment_syms_base: Every primitive (alloc, free, copy, refcount op, lock op, refcount type, lock
type) carries the **syms.json base shape**: `{name, kind, linked_in,
declared_in[], defined_in, type}`. The `kind` field uses the same 10-value
typedefs/structs that aren't classifiable as a `kind` (plain typedefs, struct
declarations). External symbols (libc, pthread, ...) carry `defined_in: null`
with `declared_in` populated. `linked_in` is composer-emitted null; future
link-time attribution may fill it. Downstream agents resolve any primitive
against the syms tree by walking
_comment_macro_variants: **Macro resolution**: a user-facing macro (e.g. `PROJ_malloc(n)` expanding to
`proj_malloc(n, __FILE__, __LINE__)`) is RESOLVED to the underlying function
symbol it expands to - there is no separate macro entry and no `expands_to`
field. Rust FFI never calls macros, so the catalogue records only the callable
function/global symbols. Resolve every allocator / dup / refcount / lock macro
to its underlying primitive before emitting.
_comment_families: **Allocator families.** One entry per deallocator/`free`. `family` is a
free-form grouping string. `free` is the syms-base entry for THE deallocator
that anchors the family. `allocators[]` is the flat list of every routine
producing a buffer this `free` releases (alloc / resize / dup alike); `copies[]`
lists the non-allocating copy primitives that write INTO this family's buffers.
A cleansing or secure deallocator (`*_clear_free`, `*_secure_free`) is a
SEPARATE family from the plain free even when they share an allocator (e.g.
`proj_zalloc` released by both `proj_free` and `proj_clear_free`): the wrapper's
drop strategy is monomorphic in the C free it calls, so a different `free`
symbol means a different `CVec<_, S>` type. The cleansing itself is done C-side
by the `*_clear_free`; the porter just binds the family's `free` (its `(ptr,
size_t)` signature carries the length). The SAME allocator may appear under
_comment_allocator_entry: An `allocators[]` element - ONE routine producing a buffer owned by this family
(released by its `free`). Each entry IS a syms-base record

not an owned constructor. A copy primitive may be listed under multiple

_comment_example: Project refcount archetype - the typical hardware-atomic-with-lock-fallback
wrapper struct most C codebases use. The wrapped int field is `val`. `atomic:
true` is the COMMON-platform truth (C11 atomics, GCC builtins, MSVC intrinsics -
whichever the build selects); `has_lock_fallback: true` records that a
non-atomic fallback exists using a lock. `fallback_lock` is the name-reference
into the `locks` list below. All primitives are typically `static inline` (kind:
function_inline_header) - Rust must call them through C wrappers
(`wrapper_inlines.c` or equivalent). `assert` carries the optional
refcount-sanity macro used in every `*_free` (typically guards against the
refcount going negative).
refcounts.note: Project refcount. Wraps an int (atomic on common platforms, lock-protected on the fallback). The standard `*_free` pattern is: NULL check -> DOWN_REF -> assert non-negative -> early-return if i > 0 -> free children -> FREE_REF -> free the struct.

_comment_example: Project RWLOCK archetype. `kind: "rwlock"` - has separate `read_lock` and
`write_lock`. `opaque: true` because the public type is typically a `typedef
void` - callers never see the underlying `pthread_rwlock_t` / `SRWLOCK`.
`reentrant: false` (POSIX rwlocks aren't reentrant by default). All primitives
are real exported functions (defined per-platform in a `threads_pthread.c` /
`threads_win.c` pair), reachable from Rust via bindgen.
locks.note: Project reader-writer lock. Opaque typedef; the underlying implementation is `pthread_rwlock_t` on POSIX, `SRWLOCK` on Windows. Used to protect refcount fallback paths and per-object internal state.

_comment_example: Standalone cleanse - zero a buffer without freeing it. Often implemented with a
volatile function pointer to memset to defeat dead-store-elimination
optimisations. Used internally by `*_clear_free` and called directly by code
that wants length-aware sensitive-data wipe without giving up the allocation.
cleansers.note: Length-aware sensitive-data wipe. Uses a volatile memset to defeat dead-store-elimination. Does NOT free.
